source.title: AutoScale: Automatic Prediction of Compute-optimal Data Composition for Training LLMs
source.authors: Fei-Yang Kang; Yi-Fan Sun; Bingbing Wen; Si Chen; D. Song; Rafid Mahmood; Ruo-Xi Jia

record.tranche_reason: The study uses power-law loss modeling and an assumed scaling relationship to build a data-mixing method, but its results evaluate domain reweighting rather than the parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling claims listed.
record.gate_note: The study reports that DDO's power-law-based predictor has 1.00% average absolute relative error, and reports loss and downstream-task results for its data-mixing methods. These evaluate the proposed domain-reweighting method, not the claim versions' scaling laws. It does not fit or test loss curves across model parameter counts or compute, or compare predicted and observed loss for much larger runs. Results about domain-mixture changes with token budget are recorded as a related finding under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study borrows a per-domain power-law form (citing Kaplan et al.) to build a data-mixing predictor, DDO. Its results evaluate domain reweighting at a fixed GPT-2 Large (774M) or BERT (110M) model size. It never fits loss against parameters, tokens or compute over orders of magnitude. It does not test extrapolation of loss to much larger runs, the compute-optimal parameter/token split, architecture shape, or downstream predictability from scale. The 1.00% average absolute relative error belongs to the study's own mixture predictor across nearby domain weights, not to a scaling-law extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that domain importance shifts with training scale, so small-scale mixtures may not transfer. Their AutoScale method speeds up perplexity reduction (28-38% for GPT-2 Large) and improves downstream results. They note the experiments are limited in scale and that projected mixtures are not proven optimal.
record.recipe_differences: This study optimizes domain weights and projects mixtures across token budgets, rather than measuring loss scaling across parameter counts, data amounts, or compute as in the original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different responses to domain reweighting for GPT-2/CLM and BERT/MLM, and reports that DDO-derived weights perform best at the scale for which they were optimized.

fits_no_version.finding: The best domain mixture shifts with token budget. DDO weights do best at the budget they were optimized for (Table 1, Figure 1 flip). Diverse domains (CommonCrawl, C4) gain share as the budget grows, while Wikipedia and ArXiv saturate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss-minimizing data-domain composition depends on the training-token budget, so mixtures chosen at small budgets may not stay optimal at larger ones.

record.problems: The authors state that their experimental settings are limited in scale and evaluation diversity, and that projected mixtures do not prove the best performance at the target scale. The reported loss results do not provide uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. DDO predictive error, AutoScale-versus-baseline speedups and downstream-task scores evaluate the proposed method rather than the listed scaling-law claims; further results are summarized in the gate_note.

untested.parts: Power-law loss in parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude; only two to four token budgets at one model size per architecture.
Prediction of loss for much larger runs from small-run fits.
Effects of depth, width or other architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss; downstream scores compare mixtures only.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on fitting choices; departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are method-comparison results at one model size. Linking all of them to 'none' is correct. The per-domain power-law fits (Fig. 10) are inputs to the method, not tests of V1 or V5.

versions.untested_parts: Loss scaling in parameters, total training tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict the loss of much larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter-count/token-count split and its growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling-law form in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or the compute-optimal parameter/token split on fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.
